title: Capsule Wardrobe Rules: 5-Piece, 3-3-3, 70/30 and More
h1: Capsule wardrobe rules compared: 5-piece, 3-3-3, Project 333 and more
excerpt: Capsule wardrobe rules compared: the 5-piece French wardrobe, 3-3-3, Project 333, 10x10, 70/30, 30 wears and 90/90, plus which rule suits whom.
tldr: Capsule wardrobe rules either limit what you wear (3-3-3, Project 333, 10x10), what you buy (the 5-piece French wardrobe, 30 wears, 70/30) or what you keep (90/90, one in, one out). Beginners do best with a short test like 10x10, over-buyers with the 5-piece rule, and overfull wardrobes with a 90/90 clear-out first.
body:
Capsule wardrobe rules are simple limits that make a small wardrobe easier to build or keep. The best known are the 5-piece French wardrobe (buy no more than five new non-basic pieces a season), the 3-3-3 rule (three tops, three bottoms, three pairs of shoes) and Project 333 (33 items for three months). Others include the 10x10 challenge, the 5-4-3-2-1 packing method, the 70/30 split, the 30 wears test and the 90/90 decluttering rule.

They don't all do the same job. Some limit what you wear, some limit what you buy, and some decide what you keep. Below is each rule in a few lines, a table to compare them, and which suits whom. If you're still at the "what does capsule wardrobe mean" stage, start with what a capsule wardrobe is and how to build one.

Capsule wardrobe rules at a glance

RuleWhat it limitsThe numbersTime frameBest for
5-piece French wardrobeWhat you buy5 new non-basic piecesPer season, usually twice a yearRegular shoppers who want to cut back without counting everything

Project 333What you wear33 items, shoes and accessories included3 monthsPeople ready for a proper experiment
10x10 challengeWhat you wear10 pieces, 10 outfits10 daysTesting the idea at no cost
5-4-3-2-1What you packAbout 15 piecesOne tripTravel
70/30 ruleThe mix70% basics, 30% personality piecesOngoingPeople who enjoy clothes

90/90 ruleWhat you keepWorn in the last 90 days or the next 90When clearing outOverfull wardrobes
One in, one outTotal sizeOne piece leaves for each that arrivesOngoingKeeping a capsule steady

What is the 5-piece capsule wardrobe rule?

The 5-piece rule, usually called the 5-piece French wardrobe, limits shopping rather than the size of your wardrobe. You start with a base of basics: plain T-shirts, jeans, trousers, knitwear, a coat. Then each season you buy at most five new pieces that aren't basics. Most versions use two seasons a year, spring/summer and autumn/winter, and as The Vivienne Files explains it, core neutral garments don't count toward the five.

The five are the pieces that give a season its character: a camel coat, a striped jumper, burgundy loafers, wide-leg wool trousers, a good leather bag. Replacing a worn-out white T-shirt doesn't use a slot. Versions differ on whether shoes and bags count, so decide that before the season starts.

Nobody has a solid claim to inventing it, and the "French" part reflects an image of owning a few good things and wearing them often rather than a documented French habit. It suits people who like shopping and want a limit they can live with. Because it doesn't cap your total, it works best after a clear-out.

If you were thinking of the 5-4-3-2-1 rule instead, that's a packing method, covered further down.

The 3-3-3 rule and Project 333 are different

The names are close, and people searching for the "333 rule" for clothes could mean either. They work very differently.

The 3-3-3 rule

Choose three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes that all work together: nine pieces. If every combination works, that's 27 possible outfits (3 × 3 × 3). It's a short experiment or a packing list, not a whole wardrobe. One week's nine might be a white T-shirt, a navy knit and an oxford shirt; dark jeans, grey trousers and stone chinos; white trainers, loafers and boots. A different "3-3-3" also circulates for styling a single outfit around colours, layers and accessories. Our 3-3-3 rule guide shows how to pick the nine.

Project 333

Courtney Carver's Project 333 asks you to dress with 33 items or fewer for three months. The 33 include clothes, shoes, accessories, jewellery and outerwear. Underwear, sleepwear, loungewear worn at home, workout clothes you actually work out in, and a wedding ring or similar sentimental piece you never take off are excluded. Everything else is boxed up for the three months, not thrown away. Our Project 333 guide covers what counts and how to set up a first season.

Short challenges: 10x10 and 5-4-3-2-1

The 10x10 challenge

Started by Lee Vosburgh of the blog Style Bee: pick 10 pieces you already own, make 10 different outfits and wear them over 10 days. Shoes usually count; underwear, socks, workout clothes and pyjamas don't. It costs nothing and quickly shows which pieces carry your outfits, which makes it a sensible first test before anything bigger.

The 5-4-3-2-1 packing rule

A travel formula: five tops, four bottoms, three pairs of shoes, two extra pieces (swimwear, dresses or layers, depending on the version) and one accessory such as a hat or bag. It gets a week into a carry-on. Our travel capsule packing guide adapts it for different kinds of trip.

Rules about balance and buying: 70/30 and 30 wears

The 70/30 rule

Keep about 70% of your wardrobe as versatile basics and let 30% be pieces that add colour, pattern or personality. It's a ratio rather than a count, so it works at any size, and some people prefer an 80/20 split. It suits anyone who finds strict capsules dull: the 30% is where the green suede trainers and the patterned shirt live. More in our 70/30 wardrobe rule explainer.

The 30 wears rule

Before buying something, ask whether you'll wear it at least 30 times. If you can't picture that, leave it. The idea is associated with sustainability campaigner Livia Firth and the #30wears hashtag, and it shifts attention from the price tag to the cost of each wear. See our 30 wears rule guide.

Rules for clearing out: 90/90 and one in, one out

The 90/90 rule

From The Minimalists: have you used this in the last 90 days, and will you use it in the next 90? If both answers are no, let it go. They're relaxed about stretching the window to 120 days or six months. For clothes, judge seasonal pieces against their own season, so a winter coat isn't failed in July. The 90/90 rule is the decluttering step in our guide to building a capsule, linked at the top of this page.

One in, one out

Every time a piece comes in, one goes. It won't build a capsule for you, but it's the simplest way to stop a finished one creeping back to its old size.

Which capsule wardrobe rule suits you?

  • Curious but unsure: try the 10x10 or a week of 3-3-3. Nothing has to leave your wardrobe.
  • Wardrobe overflowing: start with the 90/90 rule, then run Project 333 for one season with the rest boxed up.
  • You buy more than you wear: the 5-piece French wardrobe caps new purchases, and the 30 wears test filters each one.
  • You love clothes and dread a uniform: use 70/30 and skip strict counts.
  • Packing for a trip: 5-4-3-2-1, or 3-3-3 for a short one.
  • Already happy with your capsule: one in, one out, plus a quick 90/90 check each season.
  • Varied dress codes, cold winters or a uniform at work: fixed numbers fit badly. Use the rules as filters and set your own count.

Rules also combine well. A realistic year might be a 90/90 clear-out in spring, a three-month Project 333 run over summer, then the 5-piece limit and the 30 wears test to keep autumn shopping in check.

Where the rules fall short

Every number on this page is somebody's personal system that caught on, not the result of research. None of them knows how often you do laundry, whether your job needs a suit, or that your winters reach minus ten. Treat the counts as starting points. The questions behind them are the part that lasts: did I wear it, will I wear it, and does it go with what I already have?

faq.q: What is the 5 capsule wardrobe rule?
faq.a: Usually it means the 5-piece French wardrobe: keep a base of basics, then buy no more than five new non-basic pieces each season, typically twice a year. Replacing worn-out basics doesn't count toward the five. It limits shopping rather than the total size of your wardrobe. Some people mean the 5-4-3-2-1 packing rule instead, which is a travel formula.

faq.q: What is the 3-3-3 rule for clothes?
faq.a: The 3-3-3 rule means choosing three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes that all work together, nine pieces in total. If every combination works, they make 27 outfits. It's used as a short wardrobe experiment or a packing method. It isn't the same as Project 333, which allows 33 items for three months.

faq.q: Is the 333 rule the same as the 3-3-3 rule?
faq.a: No. Project 333, sometimes called the 333 rule, is Courtney Carver's challenge to wear 33 items or fewer, including shoes and accessories, for three months. The 3-3-3 rule is a much smaller set of nine pieces: three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes. The first is a seasonal wardrobe; the second is a short test or a packing list.

faq.q: What is the 70/30 rule for a wardrobe?
faq.a: The 70/30 rule says roughly 70% of your wardrobe should be versatile basics and 30% can be pieces that add colour, pattern or personality. It's a ratio rather than an item count, so it works at any wardrobe size. It suits people who want some structure without a strict limit. Some people use an 80/20 split instead.

A capsule wardrobe is a small set of clothes chosen so that most pieces go with each other, letting you make many outfits from fewer items. London boutique owner Susie Faux popularised the term in the 1970s. Most capsules are reviewed each season and hold roughly 25 to 40 pieces, though rules like Project 333 set an exact number.

faq.q: Can you combine capsule wardrobe rules?
faq.a: Yes, and many work better together. Rules that limit what you wear, such as Project 333, pair well with rules that limit what you buy, such as the 5-piece French wardrobe or the 30 wears test. A clear-out rule like 90/90 is a good first step before any of them, and one in, one out keeps the result steady afterwards.
